Field surveys conducted in Turkish coastal streams indicate that newly hatched ammocoetes of Lampetra lanceolata emerge with a remarkably low wet weight of approximately 0.00029 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00029 grams], a value that reflects the limited yolk provisioning during embryonic development. This initial mass, derived from an egg diameter of about 0.821 millimeters, places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum among European lampreys. As larvae begin filter-feeding within fine-grained sediments, they undergo a prolonged growth phase, gradually accumulating somatic tissue. Studies tracking growth trajectories in captive-reared individuals have documented that the wet weight at puberty for this species reaches about 2.7 grams [Wwp = about 2.7 grams], a mass that typically coincides with the onset of metamorphosis. This ten-thousand-fold increase from the hatching stage to puberty highlights the substantial energetic demands of larval life, during which individuals must sequester sufficient lipid reserves to fuel the non-feeding migratory adult phase. The transition to a reproductively active state therefore represents a critical energetic bottleneck in the life cycle of this imperiled species.

Reproductive output in Turkish brook lamprey has been quantified from gravid females collected during the spawning run, with the total number of eggs at the end of life estimated at 1,898.5 eggs  when individuals are maintained under controlled thermal conditions of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This fecundity value is relatively modest compared to anadromous lampreys but aligns with expectations for a purely freshwater species with limited body size. The eggs, which are deposited in shallow gravel nests dug by both sexes in swift-flowing stretches of streams, experience an incubation period that varies with ambient temperature. At the mean thermal regime typical of natal streams, the period from egg fertilisation to the onset of exogenous feeding encompasses several weeks. The yolk-dependent embryo consumes its substantial yolk reserves during this interlude, and upon yolk-sac resorption, the emerging larva begins its first feeding as a filter-feeder. This trophic switch marks the beginning of the extended juvenile phase that may persist for several years before metamorphosis.

The lifespan of the Turkish brook lamprey has been determined from mark-recapture studies and analysis of statolith bands in populations inhabiting temperate streams. Maximum recorded longevity in this species reaches 1,460 days [am = 1,460 days] under the typical thermal conditions of its native habitat, which average 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This relatively compressed lifespan, equivalent to approximately four years, is characteristic of non-parasitic lampreys that forego an extended marine feeding phase. The ammocoete larval stage dominates this period, occupying roughly three to four years before metamorphosis triggers the transformation into the sexually maturing adult. Following this transformation, the reproductively active adult exists for only a few months, during which it undertakes upstream migration, spawns, and subsequently experiences natural mortality. The brevity of the adult stage underscores the extreme semelparous life-history strategy of this species, wherein all somatic resources are shunted into a single, terminal reproductive event.

Sexual maturation in Lampetra lanceolata is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size rather than a fixed chronological age. Field measurements indicate that individuals typically reach puberty when they achieve a total length of 13 centimeters [Lp = 13 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds broadly with the wet weight at puberty of approximately 2.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.7 grams]. This length-based trigger for gonadal maturation ensures that only individuals with adequate somatic reserves initiate the costly metamorphic process. The ultimate total length attained over the course of a lifetime reaches about 17.3 centimeters [Li = about 17.3 centimeters], a value that represents the maximum size recorded in wild-caught adults. This modest ultimate size, combined with the early onset of reproductive investment at 13 centimeters, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over extended somatic growth. Comparative data from related species such as Lampetra planeri indicate that this growth pattern is conserved among brook lampreys, likely reflecting constraints imposed by the finite energy stores available to non-feeding adults during their brief spawning migration.

Rearing experiments conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have provided additional insights into the growth dynamics of this species. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 9.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 9.4 grams], a figure that represents the maximum body mass recorded in well-fed individuals approaching the end of their larval phase. This asymptotic mass, together with the total length at puberty and the wet weight at puberty, describes a growth trajectory that decelerates markedly as individuals approach metamorphic competence. Energetic modeling based on these empirical measurements confirms that the species follows a pattern typical of capital breeders, wherein resources acquired during the larval feeding stage are subsequently mobilized to support metamorphosis, upstream migration, gametogenesis onset, and the single spawning event. The longevity of approximately 1,460 days [am = approximately 1,460 days] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] therefore encapsulates a life cycle in which roughly 90 percent of the lifespan is devoted to the growing juvenile phase, with the remaining 10 percent allocated to the non-feeding adult stage culminating in reproductive senescence and physiological death.
